title: Workflow and Job Concurrency
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of workflow and job concurrency and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to workflow and job concurrency.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on workflow and job concurrency. Concurrency groups coordinate overlapping workflow/job runs and can cancel outdated work when that behavior is safe for the workload. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Workflow and Job Concurrency matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Concurrency groups coordinate overlapping workflow/job runs and can cancel outdated work when that behavior is safe for the workload. Use `needs` for dependencies, matrices for controlled combinations, conditions for deliberate branching, and concurrency/timeouts to prevent stale or unbounded work.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Concurrency groups coordinate overlapping workflow/job runs and can cancel outdated work when that behavior is safe for the workload. Use `needs` for dependencies, matrices for controlled combinations, conditions for deliberate branching, and concurrency/timeouts to prevent stale or unbounded work. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: The concurrency keyword
items.text: Measure duration, resource/runner consumption, queue time, and failure rate before changing the pipeline. Bound retries, cancel stale work only when safe, and compare the result after one controlled change.

items.title: Concurrency groups
items.text: Measure duration, resource/runner consumption, queue time, and failure rate before changing the pipeline. Bound retries, cancel stale work only when safe, and compare the result after one controlled change.

items.title: Cancelling outdated workflow runs
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Preventing overlapping deployments
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Queueing and cancellation behavior
items.text: For queueing and cancellation behavior, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Choosing concurrency group names
items.text: Measure duration, resource/runner consumption, queue time, and failure rate before changing the pipeline. Bound retries, cancel stale work only when safe, and compare the result after one controlled change.

content_blocks.code:
concurrency:
  group: deploy-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: false
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Replace with a controlled deployment step"
content_blocks.expected_output: Runs using the same group are serialized; an in-progress run is not automatically cancelled by this setting.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Add the top-level concurrency block to a test workflow and inspect behavior with two runs on the same ref. Use environment-specific group names for deployments.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet and remove temporary workflow changes. If you triggered a real run, inspect the run log before editing the file again.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to workflow and job concurrency. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain workflow and job concurrency, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Express dependencies and parallel work as a clear job graph with bounded execution and failure behavior.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Concurrency groups coordinate overlapping workflow/job runs and can cancel outdated work when that behavior is safe for the workload. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
